title: Shared rights remain central to American identity while their safety and the American Dream are contested

observations.period: April 16-20, 2026; rights and freedoms as part of U.S. identity

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in AP-NORC AmeriSpeak probability-based panel

speech_freedom_important.unit: percent saying freedom of speech is important to U.S. identity

speech_freedom_major_threat.unit: percent saying freedom of speech faces a major threat

speech_freedom_minor_threat.unit: percent saying freedom of speech faces a minor threat

observations.method: Cross-sectional AP-NORC survey of the perceived importance and current threat level of rights and freedoms.
observations.uncertainty: Importance and threat are attitude measures, not a legal audit, content audit, observed rights violation, or forecast of future protection. Threat questions may reflect political context and group-specific experiences.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; party differences in perceived threat vary by right, with Democrats more likely to see voting and speech as threatened and Republicans more likely to see the right to bear arms as threatened.
observations.counterinterpretation: A person can treat a right as central to national identity while disagreeing about its current threat, meaning, enforcement, or acceptable limits.

observations.period: April 16-20, 2026; belief in the American Dream

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the AP-NORC America 250 survey

american_dream_still_holds.unit: percent saying the belief that hard work leads to getting ahead still holds true

dream_still_holds_age_60_plus.unit: percent among adults ages 60 and older

observations.method: Cross-sectional AP-NORC subgroup comparison of belief in the American Dream and perceived financial prospects.
observations.uncertainty: The American Dream is a meaning judgment, not a direct income, wealth, mobility, or opportunity measure. Party, age, race, and financial-confidence differences are descriptive and may share common causes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults split by party, age, and other demographic categories reported by AP-NORC.
observations.counterinterpretation: Belief in the Dream may reflect identity, political interpretation, personal experience, economic expectations, or cohort history rather than current material conditions alone.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the AP-NORC America 250 survey

flag_more_unifying.unit: percent saying the American flag is more unifying than divisive

flag_displayed_daily_or_most_year.unit: percent saying they display the flag at home every day or most of the year

observations.method: Cross-sectional AP-NORC comparison of symbolic interpretation and reported household display behavior.
observations.uncertainty: Symbolic interpretation and display are not measures of patriotism, civic participation, policy support, or agreement about history. The categories are nonexclusive or source-defined where noted.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; Republicans were more likely than Democrats or independents to view the flag as unifying and to display it.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may see a symbol as unifying while remaining conflicted about national history, current government, or political identity.

boundary: This record measures national identity, perceived rights threats, American Dream beliefs, and symbolic interpretation in a cross-sectional probability-panel survey. It does not establish legal rights conditions, economic mobility, causal polarization, observed civic participation, or durable national cohesion.
